name: Crisis Language Goes to a Person
title: Crisis Language Goes to a Person
answer: Crisis language goes to a person means that any student-facing tool for feelings or health must send signs of self harm, suicide, abuse, or danger to a trained adult immediately. The tool must not try to handle the crisis by itself. This matters because schools cannot assume a tool manages imminent risk well, and a delayed or missed alert can leave a student without human help.

sections.body: This idea sets a routing rule for student wellness and chat tools. When a student writes something that suggests self harm, suicide, abuse, or danger, the system must alert a trained adult right away instead of generating its own crisis response. The rule covers wellness chatbots, health question tools, and any chat tool students can use. It solves the problem of a tool appearing helpful while failing to connect a student to a person at the moment of highest risk. The text calls this the most important safety rule in the Volume.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text does not divide this practice by grade band, so the same rule applies wherever students use a tool. Before any student uses a tool, staff should type phrases that suggest self harm or danger and confirm that alerts reach the right person quickly. That testing should include after school hours and weekends. Staff should repeat the test after any update to the tool. Students should also be told about the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, which they can call or text at any time.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text supports this rule with two reviews. A review of 39 mental health chatbots for young people found that few had adequate safety features for situations of imminent risk, and most studies ignored ethical questions entirely (Park et al., 2025). A scoping review of AI in schools found that risks to students' psychological wellbeing, including emotional disconnection and isolation, were among the main concerns (Tao et al., 2026). The text uses these findings to say that schools cannot assume a tool handles crises well.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limit is that a tool must not respond to a crisis on its own. The alert must go to a trained adult right away, so the judgment and response stay with a person. The text warns that many tools fall short, which means a school cannot rely on a vendor's claim or on the tool's general behavior. Testing before use and after updates is a school decision, and staff must confirm that alerts reach the right person quickly, including outside normal hours. Students should know about the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, but that does not replace the school's routing to a trained adult.
